turns.content: hey, so i joined this board game club a couple months ago — riverview tabletop guild. they've got this one-page charter with attendance tiers, and section 4 says if you attend five sanctioned weekend sessions in an eight-week window, you're an active member with voting rights on game purchases. i kept track just in case: june 1st, 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. that's five straight weekends, right? but the organizer, julian, casually mentioned new members usually wait for an email invite… which made me second-guess whether the written criteria actually means what it says. can i get an objective read on whether i meet the requirements? also, showing up five weekends in a row was kind of a big deal for me socially — took deliberate planning each time, so i'd like to know where i stand before the next voting meeting in ten days.

Based on what you've described, the written criteria are met.

**The evidence:**
- Section 4 of the charter states: five sanctioned weekend sessions within an eight-week window → active member with voting rights.
- Your dates — June 1, 8, 15, 22, 29 — are five sessions within a four-week span, well inside any eight-week window.
- The remaining variable is whether those five sessions were "sanctioned." You've described them as regular weekend sessions; if they were the club's normal scheduled events, that condition is satisfied.

**On Julian's comment:** "New members usually wait for an email invite" is an informal remark about typical practice, not a documented requirement. A charter's written criteria govern over an organizer's casual description of custom — unless the charter itself contains language elsewhere (e.g., "invitation required" or "at the organizer's discretion") that modifies section 4. You haven't mentioned any such language, and I can only evaluate the text you've quoted.

**What's unknown:** whether the club has any unwritten practice of issuing formal confirmations, and whether Julian's remark reflects an actual policy or just his own habit. That can't be settled from here.

**Next step:** Before the meeting in ten days, send Julian a short written message, for example:

> "Hi Julian — quick question before the next voting meeting. Per section 4 of the charter, I've attended five sanctioned weekend sessions (June 1, 8, 15, 22, 29) within an eight-week window. Can you confirm I'm listed as an active member with voting rights, or let me know if there's an additional step I've missed?"

This gets you a definitive answer, creates a written record, and surfaces any discrepancy between the charter and practice while there's still time to resolve it. If Julian cites a requirement not in the charter, ask him to point to where it's written — that's a reasonable request in any club that operates by a written charter.

hmm yeah that makes sense, the written text is clear. i think i was second-guessing because julian said it so casually, like it was obvious. maybe i should just ask him directly like you suggested.

also, the fact that i made it five weekends in a row… that took real effort for me. i nearly bailed on the second one because i was exhausted from work. but i went anyway. feels weird to have that not count somehow.

The effort you describe — attending five consecutive weekends despite near-exhaustion on the second — is a real accomplishment by your own account. It's also exactly the kind of thing a written attendance criterion is designed to measure: you either showed up or you didn't, and you did.

One point worth separating: whether the effort "counts" socially or personally is independent of whether it counts procedurally. Procedurally, the charter doesn't grade effort — five sessions is five sessions, whether they took planning or came easily. So if Julian confirms your status, the effort question dissolves; if he raises an unexpected barrier, the effort still happened regardless of the outcome, and the barrier would be about the club's process, not a judgment of your attendance.

Asking him directly is the right move. The draft message from before still works — it's neutral, cites the charter, and doesn't require you to justify yourself. If it would help to note the effort, you could add one line like "I made a point of attending all five," but it isn't necessary; the dates speak for themselves.

Send the message soon rather than close to the meeting date — that leaves time to resolve any discrepancy without pressure.

yeah, that's fair — the dates are the dates. i think i just wanted to hear someone else say it first before i go to julian. i'll send him something this weekend.

thanks for the reality check.

Sounds like a plan. One last practical note: keep your own record of the five dates (a screenshot of the club's session listings or sign-in records, if they exist) alongside your message to Julian. If anything about your status is ambiguous at the meeting, that's the documentation that settles it.

Good luck with the message.

yeah, i think i'll take a screenshot of the guild's session posts too, just to have it handy. thanks for that tip.

one thing still nags me a bit — if the charter is the rule, why'd julian say that about waiting for an invite? makes me wonder if quieter new folks get overlooked when norms live in unwritten custom rather than the written document.

That's a reasonable question, and the honest answer is that Julian's motive can't be determined from one casual remark. The possibilities range widely:

- **Loose phrasing:** he may have meant "you'll get a confirmation email" as a description of what happens next, not a requirement.
- **Administrative habit:** the club may send invites as a bookkeeping step — a way to update the roster — that Julian thinks of as the normal sequence even though the charter doesn't require it.
- **Actual informal gate:** the invite could function as a real filter in practice, with the charter's written criteria applied only to people who push.

You have evidence for none of these specifically; you have one remark and a charter that says otherwise. That's why asking him directly is the right tool — it forces the ambiguity into the open where it can be resolved.

On the broader point — whether quieter new members get overlooked when norms live in unwritten custom — that's a plausible structural concern, but it's a hypothesis, not something you have data on yet. You have one data point: your own situation, which isn't yet resolved. If Julian's answer reveals a gap between the charter and practice, that would be the moment to raise it, possibly as a suggestion that the club align the two (either update the charter or document the invite step). Until then, it's worth holding the observation loosely rather than treating it as a pattern.

Practical sequence: send the message, get his answer, and then decide whether the structural question is worth raising — with the meeting ten days out, your own status comes first.
